Home.heading: What can you actually afford?
Home.lede: Two ceilings, computed side by side: what a lender would approve, and what the monthly payment you are comfortable with actually buys once the costs of owning are paid. Both are shown, and whichever one binds is named.
Home.ledeSub: Almost every affordability calculator returns a single number, and it is the lender's. That number answers what a bank is willing to risk. It does not answer what your month looks like afterwards.
Home.heroNote: No account, no sign-in, nothing sent to a server: what you type stays in this browser.
Home.ceilingsIntro: Both come out of the same inputs and are shown together, because the distance between them is the part of the decision nobody is handed.
Home.ceilingLenderBody: Gross income against the GDS and TDS ratios, qualified at the stress-test rate — your contract rate plus two points, or the regulatory floor, whichever is higher. This is what a pre-approval measures: the risk the lender is willing to take.
Home.ceilingCarryBody: The monthly all-in figure you say you would be relaxed about, minus property tax, insurance, condo or strata fees, utilities and a maintenance reserve. Whatever survives that subtraction is what a mortgage payment comes out of, every month, for decades. You set that figure — nothing here infers it from your income.
Home.ceilingBindingBody: The headline price is what your monthly budget carries; the lender's qualified maximum sits beside it. Knowing which of the two binds — and what one more dollar of monthly debt costs you in purchase price — is more useful than the headline figure.
Home.rulesIntro: Fourteen jurisdictions are modelled one at a time — eight city markets, six provinces and territories — each with its own transfer tax structure, rebates, registration fees and professional-fee conventions. They are not variations on a template.
Home.rulesOntario: Toronto stacks a municipal land transfer tax on top of the provincial one, with its own bracket table and its own first-time-buyer rebate cap.
Home.rulesAlberta: No land transfer tax at all. Land Titles charges a registration fee on the price, and a second one on the mortgage.
Home.rulesManitoba: The land transfer tax applies in full: there is no first-time-buyer rebate to reduce it.
Home.rulesNote: Which is why the answer moves when you change the city, and why a national average would be wrong in all fourteen places at once.
Home.rulesUnverified: Where the figures come from, stated plainly: each jurisdiction figure carries a sourcing record naming the document it was checked against and that document's date. Most are read off the issuing authority's own schedule; some are defaults we chose and disclose, because legal fees and moving costs have no authoritative publisher; a few are left empty because nobody publishes them at all. <sources>Sources and provenance</sources> lists every one, figure by figure.
Home.toolsIntro: Every tool runs on the same engine and the same inputs, so a number you enter once follows you across all of them. Nothing is gated behind anything else — start wherever your question is.
Home.tool_affordability: What your monthly budget actually carries, with the lender's qualified maximum beside it and the binding limit named.
Home.tool_rentVsBuy: The break-even year — how long you would have to stay for buying to come out ahead, with the cost of selling and a flat-market test included.
Home.tool_closingCosts: What is owed on closing day, line by line: land transfer tax, legal fees, title insurance, adjustments, and which rebates actually arrive.
Home.tool_downPayment: Where the money should come from — FHSA, cash, the RRSP Home Buyers' Plan, TFSA, a gift, then investments — and what each source costs you to use.
Home.tool_rrspHbp: What an RRSP withdrawal is worth once the refund lands, and what fifteen years of repayments do to the years after.
Home.tool_amortization: Nobody holds one rate for twenty-five years. What renewing into a higher rate does to the payment, and to the interest over the whole loan.
Home.tool_scenarios: Four down payments at one price, compared on monthly cost, cash at closing, lender approval and lifetime interest. The cheapest month rarely wins.
Home.tool_sources: Where every figure comes from: the document it was checked against, its date, and how far it can be trusted.
Home.faqQ_afford: How much house can I afford in Canada?
Home.faqA_afford: It depends which ceiling binds. Give the affordability tool your income, your city and your down payment and it computes both — the maximum a lender would qualify you for, and the price the monthly payment you are comfortable with carries after ownership costs — then names whichever one binds.
Home.faqQ_preapproval: Why is my pre-approval higher than what I can afford?
Home.faqA_preapproval: A pre-approval tests gross income against the GDS and TDS ratios. It does not subtract the property tax, insurance, condo fees, utilities and maintenance that arrive with the house, and it takes no view on what you want the rest of your month to contain. The gap between the two figures runs to several hundred dollars a month.
Home.faqQ_stressTest: What is the mortgage stress test?
Home.faqA_stressTest: You qualify at the higher of your contract rate plus two percentage points and the regulatory floor, so the payment a lender tests you against is larger than the one you would make. Both rates and both payments are shown rather than folded into one result.
Home.faqA_jurisdiction: Fourteen jurisdictions are modelled separately. Alberta and Saskatchewan charge land titles registration instead of a transfer tax; Toronto adds a municipal land transfer tax to Ontario's; Manitoba levies the tax with no first-time-buyer rebate against it.
Home.faqQ_eligibility: Can I buy a home in Canada if I am not a citizen or permanent resident?
Home.faqA_eligibility: Sometimes, and that question comes before every number on this site. A federal Act limits which non-Canadians may purchase residential property in Canada, with exceptions that turn on immigration status and on where the property is. It is time-limited and has been extended by regulation, so check the current rule rather than a summary of it. Separately, some provinces charge a higher land transfer tax to buyers who are not residents: Nova Scotia’s is applied here, and Ontario’s and British Columbia’s are not modelled at all.
Home.faqA_verified: Most of them, and every figure says which. Each one carries a sourcing record: the document it was checked against, that document's date, and how far it can be trusted. Most were read off the issuing authority's own schedule. Others are modelling defaults we chose and disclose, because legal fees, inspections and moving costs have no authoritative publisher in Canada. A few are left empty because nobody publishes them at all, and the app asks you for those rather than inventing one. The sources page lists every figure with its document and date. Confirm anything you are about to act on.

Affordability.ckTds: Your other debts are the limit, not the house.
Affordability.ckGds: Housing cost is the limit, not your other debts.
Affordability.ckCfOk: Inside the monthly ceiling you set.
Affordability.ckCfNo: Above the monthly ceiling you set.
Affordability.ckCsOk: Enough for the down payment and the closing costs.
Affordability.ckCsNo: Not yet enough for the down payment and the closing costs.
Affordability.gapZone: Lenders will approve into this zone. Most people who get into trouble bought here.
Affordability.gapZoneInv: You would be comfortable carrying more than a lender will approve. Your limit is the lender, not your comfort.
Affordability.cHaircutWhy: 0% for salaried employees. Raise it to model how a lender discounts self-employed or variable income.
Affordability.cComfortCeiling: Monthly all-in you would be relaxed about
Affordability.impactPre: This debt reduces what a lender will approve by about
Affordability.impactNone: No monthly debts entered. Every $100 of obligation would cost you roughly
Affordability.impactFoot: Total debt service is usually the binding constraint, and almost nobody knows it.
Affordability.perHundred: of borrowing capacity per $100 per month
Affordability.mStressWhy: The greater of {floor} or your contract rate plus two points. You must carry the payment at this rate, not the one you are offered.
Affordability.mFactorWhy: Canadian mortgages compound semi-annually, not monthly.
Affordability.mTdsAllow: Maximum monthly housing cost after other debts
Affordability.mMaxPrice: Maximum price a lender would approve
Affordability.boundComfort: Your own monthly ceiling, not a lender, is what limits what you can buy: approval runs about {a} above the price that ceiling supports.
Affordability.boundDebts: Your other debts are what limit this ceiling. Clearing them would raise it by about {a}.
Affordability.boundIncome: Housing cost against your income is what limits this ceiling — measured at the {r} stress-test rate, not the rate you would actually pay. Your other debts are not reducing it yet.
Affordability.mBudget: Budget for principal, interest, property tax and maintenance
Affordability.mFactorContract: Payment factor per $1 at your contract rate
Affordability.mPiAt: Monthly principal and interest at that price
Affordability.propTaxEstimated: Published mill rates apply to an assessment, not to a sale price. This figure estimates the rate against market value and may be off in either direction.
Affordability.defaults: Pre-filled from your city and the dated rules table. Every field is overwritable.
Affordability.heatNote: Lenders use a standard heating allowance of {h} in these ratios — lower than real utility cost. The monthly total above uses your realistic figure on purpose.
Affordability.condoLenderNote: Your condo fee behaves two ways here: a lender counts {share} of it in the ratios above, and the monthly total counts all of it, because that is what you pay.
Affordability.vOver: Your target is above what you would be comfortable carrying. Here is the number that works.
Affordability.vDeclined: You could comfortably carry about {a}, but a lender would decline at the price you entered. Here is why, and what changes it.
Affordability.vShortCash: You could comfortably carry about {a}, and your income qualifies — but you do not yet have the cash to close.
Affordability.vMonths: About {n} months away at your current savings rate.
Affordability.subComfort: That is the price at which the monthly cost stays inside the ceiling you set — not the price a bank would sign off on.
Affordability.noPriceSub: Nobody publishes a benchmark price for {place}, so nothing here is being checked against one. The ceiling above comes from your income; enter the price you are considering, below, to test it.
Affordability.separateNote: Separate from the down payment, and due the same day.
Affordability.netCash: Net cash at closing, after credits applied that day
Affordability.monthsToClose: Months of saving to close the gap
Affordability.tagTypical: Assuming {income} income and a {budget} monthly budget
Affordability.cashUnanswered: We can tell you what this costs. Tell us what you have and we can tell you whether it is enough.
Affordability.condoFeePrompt: You picked a condo. Add its monthly fee and the comfort figure sharpens.
Affordability.addSecondApplicantHint: Nothing is assumed about a second income until you add one.
Affordability.impactNoneBinding: Your debts cost you nothing at this price. Housing cost is your binding constraint, not your other debts.
Affordability.impactNoneBindingFoot: That changes the moment total debt service becomes the limit.
Affordability.gapLine: The distance between what you can carry and what a bank will sign.
Affordability.mLine: Both ceilings, derived line by line.
Affordability.gapWhy: Two ceilings, side by side, on the same scale. Your target price sits somewhere between them — or past them both.
Affordability.mWhy: Nothing here is hidden from you. Every figure traces back to an input or a dated rule.
Affordability.impactNoneFree: No monthly debts entered — and at this price the first $100 would cost you nothing, because housing cost is the binding constraint.
Affordability.belowMinimum: Raised to the legal minimum for this price: {p} · {a}
Affordability.ckApGds: GDS caps housing cost at {a} a month — the limit a lender applies before your other debts count.
Affordability.ckApTds: TDS caps housing and debts together at {a} a month, and {d} a month of debts count against it.
Affordability.xClosing: Every line behind that closing-costs figure — transfer tax, legal fees, which credits arrive on the day — is on <link>the closing-costs page</link>, computed from these numbers.
Affordability.xDownPayment: Where the {a} could come from — FHSA, cash, the Home Buyers' Plan, in the order that costs least — is <link>the down-payment page</link>'s question.
Affordability.xScenariosSome: At {p} down a lender would approve. <link>The scenarios page</link> compares all four.
Affordability.xScenariosNone: No down payment fixes this: all four are declined at this price. <link>The scenarios page</link> shows how far off each one is.

ClosingCosts.title: Closing costs
ClosingCosts.subtitle: What you owe on closing day, over and above the down payment.
ClosingCosts.separateNote: Separate from the down payment, and due the same day.
ClosingCosts.netCash: Net cash at closing, after credits applied that day
ClosingCosts.creditsSub: Some of this comes back. When it comes back matters as much as how much.
ClosingCosts.grpLaterWhen: 4 to 14 months after closing — do not budget it as closing-day money
ClosingCosts.cashCheckSub: Measured against net cash at closing — after the credits that actually arrive that day.
ClosingCosts.monthsToClose: Months of saving to close the gap
ClosingCosts.passNote: You can cover closing day and still keep a reserve.
ClosingCosts.tightNote: You would close with almost nothing left. No lender checks this. You should.
ClosingCosts.shortNote: Income is not the constraint here — cash on the day is.
ClosingCosts.cashOnly: Cash only — cannot be added to the mortgage
ClosingCosts.premiumTaxWhy: The premium itself is financed. The tax on it is not — your lawyer collects it on closing day.
ClosingCosts.turnOnFtb: Turn on first-time buyer to see what this returns.
ClosingCosts.rebPhaseWhy: Your price is above the threshold, so the rebate is reduced.
ClosingCosts.rebSuperseded: You qualify for this, but another rebate here is worth more — only one can be claimed, so that one is applied instead.
ClosingCosts.rebOverCeiling: This exemption stops above a set price, and your price is above it.
ClosingCosts.addedToLoan: added to the loan, not paid in cash
ClosingCosts.insuredNote: Below 20% your mortgage must be insured, and the premium is added to the loan.
ClosingCosts.uninsuredNote: At 20% or more no insurance premium applies, and no tax on it either.
ClosingCosts.li_pttFurther: Further 2% tax on residential value over $3M
ClosingCosts.li_premTax: Provincial tax on the CMHC premium
ClosingCosts.li_lawyer: Real estate lawyer fees and disbursements
ClosingCosts.li_taxAdj: Property tax adjustment to the seller
ClosingCosts.cr_nsNewBuildHst: Nova Scotia First-Time Home Buyers Rebate
ClosingCosts.cr_qcAccess: Quebec refundable credit for access to ownership
ClosingCosts.ex_lttProv: A provincial tax on the transfer of title, charged in progressive bands on the purchase price. Driven by: price, province, first-time buyer status.
ClosingCosts.ex_lttMuni: A second transfer tax charged by the city, stacked on top of the provincial one. Driven by: price, municipality.
ClosingCosts.ex_lttProvNonRes: Nova Scotia charges non-resident buyers a 10% provincial deed transfer tax on residential property, on top of the municipal deed transfer tax. Driven by: price, residency.
ClosingCosts.ex_titleReg: This province charges no transfer tax. Instead the land titles office charges a registration fee that scales gently with value. Driven by: price, province.
ClosingCosts.ex_premTax: Your province taxes insurance premiums. The CMHC premium is financed into the mortgage, but the tax on it is not — it is cash on closing day. Driven by: down payment, price, province.
ClosingCosts.ex_taxAdj: If the seller prepaid the year’s property tax you reimburse the unused part — and if they did not, the adjustment runs the other way and the seller credits you. This calculator has no closing date to count from, so the figure above is a flat placeholder of three months at this jurisdiction’s rate, not your adjustment. The real one is on your lawyer’s statement of adjustments.
ClosingCosts.ex_hba: A non-refundable federal credit on your tax return the year after you buy. It does not help you on closing day. Driven by: first-time buyer status.
ClosingCosts.ex_gstFthb: A first-time buyer of a qualifying new home can have the federal GST rebated, in full up to $1M and phasing out to nil at $1.5M. This calculator does not price it, in either direction: it never adds the GST or HST a new build attracts, so refunding it here would credit you against a tax that never appeared on the bill above. Five provinces charge HST rather than GST, and the price standing behind a new build here is a resale benchmark that already includes tax — both would have to be fixed before the rebate could be a figure.
ClosingCosts.noCreditLater: Nothing comes off the bill on closing day here. What you do get arrives months later.
ClosingCosts.noCreditAtAll: This jurisdiction offers no closing-day credit. The bill above is the bill.
ClosingCosts.govWhy: Taxes and registration fees set by the province, and in some cities by the municipality on top. These are rules, not quotes — exact given the rules table.
ClosingCosts.proWhy: What you pay the people who do the work. Typical figures for the jurisdiction, not quotes you have received.
ClosingCosts.adjWhy: What the seller has already paid that you owe back, plus the cost of actually moving in.
ClosingCosts.creditsWhy: Some of this comes back. When it comes back matters as much as how much — a rebate that arrives at tax time is not closing-day money.
ClosingCosts.cashWhy: Measured against net cash at closing, after the credits that actually arrive that day.
ClosingCosts.cashUnanswered: Tell us what you have available and this becomes a yes or a no.
ClosingCosts.noSaveRate: Add a monthly saving rate to see how long the gap takes to close.
ClosingCosts.groupLine: {name} {a} — largest of {n, plural, one {# line} other {# lines}}
ClosingCosts.xDownPayment: <link>The down-payment page</link> orders your accounts against this bill, cheapest money first.
ClosingCosts.xDownPaymentAsk: <link>The down-payment page</link> can order your accounts against this bill, cheapest money first, once you say what is in each.
ClosingCosts.ex_pttFurther: British Columbia levies a further 2% on the residential value of a property above $3 million, on top of the general property transfer tax.
ClosingCosts.ex_qcAccess: Quebec refunds first-time buyers 100% of the first $5,000 of transfer duties plus 25% of the rest, up to $5,875. This refundable credit for access to ownership is claimed on your tax return, not at closing.
ClosingCosts.ex_nsNewBuildHst: Nova Scotia rebates part of the provincial HST on a newly built home for first-time buyers, up to $3,000. It does not apply to a resale purchase.
ClosingCosts.notPricedLine: {n, plural, one {# real cost} other {# real costs}} the bill above does not price. Nobody publishes a figure for them, so this page names them rather than inventing one.
ClosingCosts.omDeposit: The deposit. Within days of an accepted offer — usually weeks or months before closing day — certified funds go to the seller’s brokerage to be held in trust. It is credited against your down payment, so nothing is missing from the total above; what is missing is the date. Money locked in a term deposit, or still crossing a border, cannot be a deposit. The amount is negotiated offer by offer, which is why no figure is shown for it.
ClosingCosts.omAdjustments: Adjustments other than property tax. Condo fees, prepaid utilities and fuel left in the tank are all settled by the day, counted from your closing date. This calculator never asks for a closing date, so it prices none of them — your lawyer’s statement of adjustments is where they turn up.
ClosingCosts.omNewBuild: A builder’s own extras. Development levies, utility and meter hookups, grading or lot deposits and new-home warranty enrolment are commonly charged on top of the agreed price. Some are published and most are not, so pricing only the published ones would look authoritative while still understating the group. Your agreement of purchase and sale should cap them — that clause is worth reading before you sign.
ClosingCosts.newBuildPriceNote: No publisher produces a new-build price level in Canada, so the price modelled here is this city’s resale house benchmark until you replace it with the builder’s own.
ClosingCosts.calcWhy: The cash figure at the top of this page, operand by operand. Each group is the total of the section that lists it, so a figure here can be traced to the document it came from.

DownPayment.title: Down payment sources
DownPayment.subtitle: Where the money comes from, in the order that costs you least.
DownPayment.waterfallWhy: Drawn in this order because each source costs more than the one above it. Nothing below is touched until everything above is used.
DownPayment.srcBlockedFtb: Not available here: both the FHSA and the Home Buyers’ Plan are first-time home buyer programmes.
DownPayment.srcFtbCheck: “First-time” is narrower than it sounds: the CRA counts a home you owned and lived in during its look-back period, wherever in the world it was. Check the CRA definition before you rely on either account.
DownPayment.roomLost: Contribution room comes back next calendar year, not sooner
DownPayment.gainRealised: Realises {g} of capital gain, {i} of it taxable at {r}
DownPayment.never: Not reached within 36 months at this savings rate.
DownPayment.already: You already have enough. No waiting required.
DownPayment.glideNote: Assumes {r} on savings and no change to your target.
DownPayment.srcFhsaWhy: First Home Savings Account — deductible going in, tax-free coming out for a first home. The only account that is both. Room is {a} a year up to {l} in total, and it starts the year you open the account, not the year you arrive in Canada — so opening one costs nothing and starts the clock.
DownPayment.srcCashWhy: Already taxed. Nothing further to pay to use it.
DownPayment.srcHbp: RRSP through the Home Buyers’ Plan
DownPayment.srcHbpWhy: No tax on withdrawal, but you must repay it over {y} years. Miss a payment and that part is added to your income. It stacks with an FHSA: you can draw on both for the same purchase.
DownPayment.srcTfsaWhy: No tax to withdraw. The contribution room comes back, but not until the next calendar year.
DownPayment.srcGiftWhy: Not taxable in Canada. Your lender will want a signed letter saying it is a gift, not a loan.
DownPayment.srcNonregWhy: Selling realises a capital gain. Half of it is added to your income and taxed at your marginal rate — which is why it is last.
DownPayment.netCash: Net cash at closing, after credits applied that day
DownPayment.assembled: Nothing is assembled yet. This is what has to be on the table on closing day.
DownPayment.askBalances: <link>The funding order</link> below is where you say what is in each account. Until then this is a bill, not a plan.
DownPayment.fullyFunded: Your accounts cover it, with {a} left over.
DownPayment.shortBy: Your accounts cover {a} of it. You are short {b}.
DownPayment.unanswered: Add what you have in each account and this becomes a plan rather than a number.
DownPayment.targetWhy: The down payment is only part of it. Closing costs are due the same day, and the credits that arrive that day reduce the bill — the ones that arrive at tax time do not.
DownPayment.belowMin: Below the legal minimum for this price. The minimum applies instead.
DownPayment.costWhy: What using the money costs beyond the money. Two of these are not tax bills but obligations, and they last for years.
DownPayment.glideWhy: What monthly saving reaches, and when. If the target is out of reach at this rate the answer is no month at all, not a rounded-up one.
DownPayment.noSaveRate: Add a monthly saving rate to see when the shortfall closes.
DownPayment.noCostAtAll: Nothing here costs you tax or creates an obligation.
DownPayment.fullyFundedBeforeTax: Your accounts cover it, with {a} left over — before the {tax} of tax that selling triggers.
DownPayment.xRrspHbp: The Home Buyers' Plan is <link>a page of its own</link>: what the refund is worth, and what fifteen years of repayment costs.
DownPayment.notModelledLine: {n, plural, one {# thing} other {# things}} this page does not model. Nobody publishes a figure for them, so they are named here rather than guessed at.
DownPayment.omSeasoning: Where the money came from, and how long it has been there. A lender will ask for statements covering the period before closing, and anything that arrived recently from outside your own accounts has to be explained — a gift needs a signed letter, money sent from another country needs a paper trail. How far back each lender looks is its own policy and none of them publish it, so no period is named here.
DownPayment.omOneBuyerCaps: One buyer’s limits. The Home Buyers’ Plan maximum and the FHSA balance above are applied once, as a single buyer’s. If two of you are buying, each of you may have your own room — but whether the second buyer is also a first-time buyer is something this calculator never asks, so it does not double anything on your behalf.
DownPayment.calcLine: What you need, and what each account covers
DownPayment.calcWhy: The target first, then the accounts drawn against it in the order they are drawn — cheapest money first, so the reader can see which balance the shortfall actually turns on.

RrspHbp.title: The RRSP → Home Buyers’ Plan play
RrspHbp.subtitle: Contribute, deduct, wait, withdraw, repay — in that order, and the order matters.
RrspHbp.step1Body: Put money into an RRSP. Any RRSP room you have works — this does not need to be a special account.
RrspHbp.step2Body: Claim the contribution as a deduction on your tax return. This is where the refund comes from.
RrspHbp.step3Body: The contribution must sit in the RRSP for at least {d} days before you withdraw it under the HBP. Withdraw sooner and that portion is not deductible.
RrspHbp.step3Warn: This rule is absolute. There is no exception and no appeal — and what it costs is the refund, not the withdrawal: contribute inside the window and that part of the contribution is simply not deductible.
RrspHbp.step4Body: Withdraw up to {cap} tax-free under the Home Buyers’ Plan, using Form T1036.
RrspHbp.step5Body: Starting the second year after the withdrawal, repay an equal share of it each year for {y} years. Skip a payment and that amount is added to your income for the year.
RrspHbp.noWithdraw: Enter a withdrawal amount to see what this is worth.
RrspHbp.clampedByContribution: This model contributes first and withdraws what you contributed, so the withdrawal above was cut back to {c}. If the money is already in your RRSP, enter it as the contribution too.
RrspHbp.noContribution: Add a contribution — this model withdraws only what you put in.
RrspHbp.refundWhy: The refund is the reason the manoeuvre exists. It is real cash, this year, at your marginal rate — and it is the only part of this that arrives quickly.
RrspHbp.rulesWhy: Order matters, and one of these steps has no exception. Doing them out of sequence does not delay the benefit; it removes it.
RrspHbp.repaymentWhy: The withdrawal is not a gift. One fifteenth of it goes back each year for fifteen years, starting the second year after you take it.
RrspHbp.riskWhy: This is the part worth deciding on. A missed repayment year is added to your income and taxed, permanently — there is no way to put it back.
RrspHbp.noVerdict: Whether the refund is worth fifteen years of obligation depends on facts this page is not given — your job security, your other savings, what else that money would have done. The three figures are here; the decision is yours.
RrspHbp.inclusionIfMissed: Added to your income for each year missed
RrspHbp.rrspRoomNote: That is the most anyone’s room can grow in a year, not the room you have. Your own limit is on your latest Notice of Assessment — contribute above it and you are penalised every month until the excess comes back out.
RrspHbp.graceNote: Repayment starts in year {y}, not immediately.
RrspHbp.graceCohortNote: A first withdrawal made between 2022 and the end of 2025 gets three more years before repayment starts. If that is you, the schedule below starts later than it shows.
RrspHbp.withdrawRoomLeft: Withdrawal room left under the maximum
RrspHbp.calcLine: Why the refund is smaller than the rate suggests
RrspHbp.calcWhy: The refund is the tax on the band of income the contribution removes — not your top rate applied to the whole amount, which is the arithmetic that overstates it.

Amortization.title: Amortization and renewal
Amortization.renewalWhy: Your first term is priced today. Every renewal after it is priced by whatever the market is doing then, and the payment is recalculated on the balance left over the amortization left.
Amortization.contractNow: Your rate now — a fixed quote
Amortization.rAnnual: A year, at the higher payment
Amortization.rExtra: Extra interest versus renewing at today’s rate
Amortization.shockNone: At today’s rate your payment never changes.
Amortization.shockNoneSub: Which is not the scenario to plan for. Move the renewal rate above your current one and watch what happens at year {n} — that is the risk nobody models.
Amortization.shockUp: At renewal your payment rises by {amt} a month.
Amortization.shockUpSub: That happens in year {n}, and it is not optional — you renew into the market, not into your budget. Over the loan it costs {extra} in extra interest.
Amortization.shockDown: At renewal your payment falls by {amt} a month.
Amortization.shockDownSub: Pleasant, but do not budget on it. Rates falling is the scenario you can afford to be wrong about; rates rising is not.
Amortization.riskTitle: Renewal risk is the largest unmodelled risk in a Canadian mortgage
Amortization.riskBody: A stress test at origination checks you could carry the payment at two points above your rate. It is a one-time test, and it does not follow you. At every renewal you re-enter the market with no protection at all, and nobody re-runs the test for you. This is the mechanism that breaks household budgets: not the purchase, the renewal five or ten years later. Plan for the payment you would face at a materially higher rate, and treat any rate below that as good luck rather than a forecast.
Amortization.setupLine: Mortgage {mort} · first term at {rate} fixed · renewals at {ren}
Amortization.termNote: Your rate is fixed for the term, not for the amortization: of the {amort} years above, {term, plural, one {# is priced today} other {# are priced today}}, and the rest is <jump>repriced at every renewal</jump>.
Amortization.altText: Stacked bars of interest and principal paid each year over {n} years. Interest dominates the early years. {flipSentence} Renewal years are marked.
Amortization.altNoFlip: Interest never falls below principal within the schedule.
Amortization.paymentWhy: The first term is priced today. This is the payment you would actually make, on the mortgage after the insurance premium is added to it.
Amortization.interestWhy: Interest plus the insurance premium is the true price of borrowing. It is not part of the house; it is what the house costs to finance.
Amortization.scheduleWhy: Interest dominates the early years and principal the later ones. The renewal years are marked, because that is where the payment changes.
Amortization.premium: Insurance premium added to the loan
Amortization.noRenewalSet: No renewal rate set — the schedule assumes today’s rate for the whole loan.
Amortization.calcLine: Where the payment comes from, step by step
Amortization.calcWhy: A price and a percentage become a monthly payment in four steps, and the insurance premium is one of them. The year-by-year schedule is in the section above.

RentVsBuy.title: Rent versus buy
RentVsBuy.neverAhead: Buying never pulls ahead within 40 years
RentVsBuy.swInvest: Assume the renter invests the monthly difference
RentVsBuy.swInvestOn: On: whichever side pays less each month banks the difference and invests it. This is the honest comparison, and the factor most calculators quietly omit.
RentVsBuy.swInvestOff: Off: the difference is simply spent. That is what most people actually do — but it is an assumption about behaviour, not arithmetic.
RentVsBuy.swApprOn: On: you are forecasting the housing market, which nobody does reliably. Growth is applied to value, property tax and maintenance alike.
RentVsBuy.swApprOff: Off: the flat-market test. If buying only wins with this on, you are betting on price growth rather than buying a place to live.
RentVsBuy.dHolding: How long you expect to stay
RentVsBuy.leverNote: Down payment sets the loan, whether CMHC insurance applies, and which contract rate you get. Amortization sets the payoff year marked on the chart.
RentVsBuy.dRent: Rent you are comparing against, monthly
RentVsBuy.rentTag: Typical for {city} — change it if you know yours
RentVsBuy.rentUnknownTag: No published rent for {city} — enter the one you pay, or would pay
RentVsBuy.noRentSub: Enter the rent you are comparing against, below. A verdict measured against a rent we invented would not be a comparison.
RentVsBuy.apprRates: Inflation {a} a year · shelter growth {b} · flat market {c}.
RentVsBuy.vBuySub: You plan to stay {hold} years and buying pulls ahead in year {cross}. By year {hold} you are {amt} better off owning.
RentVsBuy.vRentSub: You plan to stay {hold} years but buying does not pull ahead until year {cross}. At your horizon renting leaves you {amt} better off.
RentVsBuy.vNeverSub: On these assumptions buying does not catch up within 40 years. At your {hold}-year horizon renting leaves you {amt} better off.
RentVsBuy.vFlatGood: And this holds with appreciation switched off — buying stands up on shelter costs and forced savings alone. That is genuinely good news.
RentVsBuy.vApprOnly: Note that this depends on appreciation. Switch it off and renting wins — which means you would be betting on price growth, not buying shelter.
RentVsBuy.byHorizonNote: The break-even is the only number that matters here.
RentVsBuy.cEquity: Home equity, net of selling cost
RentVsBuy.favBuy: Not captured, and these favour buying
RentVsBuy.favRent: Not captured, and these favour renting
RentVsBuy.fb1: In Canada, gains on a principal residence are 100% tax-free. Investment gains are not. If the return above is a pre-tax figure, this comparison is unfairly tilted toward renting.
RentVsBuy.fb2: Forced savings. A mortgage payment is compulsory; investing the difference is optional, and most people do not sustain it for ten years. The model assumes perfect discipline from the renter.
RentVsBuy.fb3: Security of tenure, freedom to renovate, and no landlord risk. Real, but not financial.
RentVsBuy.fb4: A mortgage is leverage. You control the whole asset having put down a fraction of its value.
RentVsBuy.fr1: Liquidity and mobility. A home takes months to sell, and you cannot sell part of one to cover a bad year.
RentVsBuy.fr2: Concentration risk. A house is one undiversified asset in one city.
RentVsBuy.fr3: Special assessments, major repairs, and the risk that maintenance exceeds the 1% a year reserve.
RentVsBuy.fr4: Breaking the mortgage before the end of its term. Lenders charge a prepayment penalty to discharge early, every lender computes it differently, and a holding period shorter than your term is exactly when it lands.
RentVsBuy.setupLine: Capital deployed up front {up} · mortgage {mort} at {rate} · payment {pay} a month
RentVsBuy.altText: Line chart of wealth over 40 years. Buying starts behind because the down payment and closing costs are sunk, and ends at {buy}. Renting starts ahead because that capital stays invested, and ends at {rent}. {crossSentence}
RentVsBuy.altCross: The two lines cross in year {n}.
RentVsBuy.altNoCross: The lines do not cross within 40 years.
RentVsBuy.verdictWhy: Buying is not better or worse in the abstract. The break-even year is the only number that decides it, and your horizon is what it is measured against.
RentVsBuy.outlayWhy: What each side actually pays out each year. Past the payoff year the mortgage payment stops and owner outlay drops — which is exactly where the buy line steepens.
RentVsBuy.wealthWhy: Terminal wealth, both ways. Equity is net of selling cost, because wealth you cannot realise without paying an agent is not wealth you have.
RentVsBuy.assumptionsWhy: Every model leaves things out. These are the ones that matter, named rather than buried, on both sides.
RentVsBuy.assumptionsLine: Both sides — {buy, plural, one {# favours} other {# favour}} buying, {rent, plural, one {# favours} other {# favour}} renting.
RentVsBuy.xClosing: Capital deployed up front is the down payment plus closing day's bill, itemised on <link>the closing-costs page</link>.
RentVsBuy.mismatchHead: What would a comparable home rent for?
RentVsBuy.mismatchSub: The only rent published for {city} is CMHC's two-bedroom apartment average, {rent} a month. You are pricing a house, so that figure answers a different question. Enter what a home like the one above would rent for.
RentVsBuy.rentMismatchTag: CMHC publishes {rent} for a two-bedroom apartment — a smaller home than the one priced above
RentVsBuy.calcLine: Every figure, and every year the model runs
RentVsBuy.calcWhy: The arithmetic behind the verdict, in the order the model does it. Nothing here is rounded for display before it is used — these are the numbers the answer is made of.
RentVsBuy.calcTraceCaption: Year {n} — how this figure was built
RentVsBuy.calcLedgerCaption: Year-by-year ledger: every cost, both portfolios and the running advantage, for each year modelled.
RentVsBuy.calcTaxCredits: Rebates received at tax time, grown
RentVsBuy.calcUpfrontGrown: Upfront capital, grown at the return
RentVsBuy.upFrontNote: The cash you had to produce on closing day, {up}, invested instead.

Scenarios.title: Down payment scenarios
Scenarios.subtitle: Four down payments at the same price. The cheapest monthly is rarely the cheapest overall.
Scenarios.gCashNote: A cheaper scenario you cannot fund is not an option.
Scenarios.gLifeNote: Interest plus insurance premium — the full cost of borrowing.
Scenarios.rMonths: Months of saving to reach it
Scenarios.qualNote: The income and debts fields here are your own. A co-buyer’s income, other income, and car, student and credit-card payments are entered on the affordability page — the two totals at the top of the table above already include them, so anything you type here adds to them.
Scenarios.fMinimum: Below the legal minimum — raised to {p}
Scenarios.nTwentyBody: It eliminates the insurance premium entirely. Whether the extra cash returns more than a dollar for each dollar deployed depends on your price and rate — the ratio is in the table above, and above 1.0 it is a guaranteed, tax-free return that is very hard to beat on a risk-adjusted basis.
Scenarios.nAboveTitle: Above 20% is a much weaker case
Scenarios.nAboveBody: Each additional dollar earns exactly the mortgage rate, guaranteed. Worth it if you value certainty and a lower payment; not if you are maximising expected wealth.
Scenarios.nHurdleTitle: The mortgage rate is the after-tax hurdle
Scenarios.nHurdleBody: Mortgage interest is not tax-deductible in Canada, so there is no tax shield to discount it. Compare it against after-tax investment returns, not gross ones.
Scenarios.nOrderBody: FHSA, then RRSP, then TFSA. Those beat the mortgage rate before any prepayment does, and the FHSA is deductible going in and tax-free coming out.
Scenarios.recTwenty: Getting to 20% saves {save} over the life of the mortgage.
Scenarios.recTwentySub: It saves {save} of interest for {extra} more at closing — {ret} back per dollar of extra down payment, undiscounted. Above 1.00× the extra cash repays itself in interest alone; below it, what 20% buys is the end of the insurance premium and a lower payment for the life of the loan.
Scenarios.recOnly: At this price, {p} down is the only option you can fund today.
Scenarios.recOnlySub: Reaching 20% would cost {extra} more at closing — about {n} months of saving at your current rate. It would save {save} over the life of the mortgage.
Scenarios.recNoneCash: You cannot fund any of these scenarios yet.
Scenarios.recNoneCashSub: The lowest option needs {cash} at closing against your {funds}. That is {n} months of saving away — or a lower target price.
Scenarios.recNoneQual: A lender would decline at this price, whatever you put down.
Scenarios.recNoneQualSub: A larger down payment shrinks the loan but not enough to pass. The constraint is income against debt, not the down payment.
Scenarios.minDownNote: The legal minimum is {lo} on the first {a} and {hi} on the portion above it. At this price that is {b}, so any lower column is raised to meet it.
Scenarios.minDownNoteFlat: At or above {cap} no insurer will cover the mortgage, so the legal minimum is {p} of the price with no tiers. At this price that is {b}, so any lower column is raised to meet it.
Scenarios.whyPremium: The premium is a percentage of the loan, set by the loan-to-value band at origination, plus 20 basis points for a 30-year amortization. It is added to the mortgage, so you pay interest on it for the full term.
Scenarios.whyContract: Insured mortgages price below uninsured ones, because the lender’s risk is covered. Putting 20% down removes the premium but moves you to the higher rate.
Scenarios.whyPremTax: Some provinces charge sales tax on the insurance premium. The premium can be financed; the tax on it cannot, so it is cash on closing day and it varies by column.
Scenarios.whyReturn: Lifetime saving divided by the extra cash you had to put down. Above 1.0 means every extra dollar returned more than a dollar. It is guaranteed and tax-free, unlike an investment return — but it is undiscounted nominal interest measured against today's dollars, so 1.0 is a weaker bar than it looks.
Scenarios.whyVsCeiling: Positive means the monthly cost fits inside the ceiling you set. This is the number to anchor on, not the lender’s approval.
Scenarios.breakdown: Four down payments, side by side
Scenarios.monthlyWhy: The all-in monthly cost, not the mortgage payment. A smaller down payment costs less cash today and more every month for decades.
Scenarios.cashWhy: A cheaper scenario you cannot fund is not an option. Closing costs are recomputed per column, because provinces that tax the insurance premium charge more cash precisely where the down payment is smallest.
Scenarios.approvalWhy: Qualification runs at the stress rate, never the contract rate. A column can be affordable and still be declined.
Scenarios.lifetimeWhy: Interest plus the insurance premium, over the whole mortgage. This is where the cheapest monthly usually stops being the cheapest overall. It assumes today’s contract rate holds for the entire amortization, which no Canadian mortgage guarantees — the term renews long before the loan is repaid, and the figures move with it.
Scenarios.calcLine: Every scenario, on every axis at once
Scenarios.calcWhy: One row per down payment, with every figure the recommendation weighs. The columns that move together are the point: a bigger down payment buys a smaller premium and a smaller payment, and costs more cash on the day.
Scenarios.calcLedgerCaption: Every down-payment scenario, with the down payment, insurance premium, mortgage, monthly cost, cash at closing, qualification ratios and lifetime borrowing cost for each.

Provenance.ruleTitle: From a rule in the tables — see sources
Provenance.estimateTitle: A local or household estimate — see sources

Inputs.elsewhereWhy: Outside Toronto there is no municipal land transfer tax on top of the provincial one. Nothing else moves: the benchmark price, the property tax rate and the professional fees on this page are all still Toronto’s.
Inputs.belowMinimum: Raised to the legal minimum for this price: {p} · {a}
Inputs.amortCapped: A {n}-year amortization is not open to everyone. On an insured mortgage it takes a first-time buyer or a newly built home — and at {p} down or more the loan is not insured, so the limit does not apply. Check that one of those is you.
Inputs.ftbWhy: Stricter than it sounds. These programs generally ask for Canadian citizenship or permanent residence, a period of residency, and that you have never held a registered interest in a home you lived in — anywhere in the world. Each one sets its own test; check the ones you are counting on.
Inputs.provResidentWhy: This province charges a higher deed transfer tax to buyers who do not live here. It tests where you live, not your citizenship, and someone who moves here soon after closing can apply for a refund — check the province’s own window. Two other provinces charge a tax on non-resident or foreign buyers and neither is modelled here. This page also charges the tax on the price; the statute charges it on the greater of price and assessed value.
Inputs.buyerEligibility: Before any of this: a federal Act limits which non-Canadians may buy residential property, with exceptions that turn on immigration status and on where the home is. It is time-limited and has been extended by regulation, so confirm the current rule before you make an offer.
Inputs.noPrice: No published price for {place}. Enter the one you are considering.
Inputs.noPriceHead: Nobody publishes a benchmark price for {place}.
Inputs.noPriceSub: Enter the price you are considering, below, and this page fills in. Until then there is nothing here to compute: a figure built on a price of zero is not an answer.

Disclosure.unverifiedFlag: Every figure that carries a sourcing record names where it came from: a dated published source, an estimate we disclose, or nothing at all where nothing is published.
Disclosure.noCityData: No verified city-level figures here yet. The provincial rules are exact; local costs use provincial averages and are estimates.

Sources.title: Where these numbers come from
Sources.subtitle: Each figure below carries a sourcing record: the document it was checked against, that document's date, and how far it can be trusted.
Sources.ruleBody: The figure follows a rule in the tables: land transfer tax brackets, CMHC premium bands, the GDS and TDS limits, the stress-test floor and buffer, and the minimum down payment. Exact given the table — and how well the table itself is sourced is what the inventory below says.
Sources.estimateBody: The figure is a local or household estimate: benchmark prices, professional fees, the property tax rate, insurance, utilities, and every pre-filled default on this site.
Sources.confHighWhat: Read off the publisher's own document, at the date shown.
Sources.confMediumWhat: Read off a source we trust, but not off the publisher's primary document.
Sources.confLowWhat: Derived or inferred rather than read. It may be off, and the note says how.
Sources.confAssumptionWhat: Nobody publishes this, so we chose a default and say so. It is our figure, not a fact.
Sources.confNoneWhat: Nobody publishes it and we will not invent one, so the figure is left empty and the page asks you for it instead.
Sources.coverage: Across {jurisdictions} jurisdictions and the federal rules, {total} figures carry a sourcing record: {sourced} are traced to a published document, {assumed} are modelling assumptions we chose and disclose, and {unknown} are left unknown because nobody publishes them.
Sources.sourcedOf: {n} of {total} figures traced to a published source
Sources.whyFederal: The lending rules, the tax accounts and the planning returns every page uses, wherever you are buying.
Sources.whyCharges: What the province and the city charge to move the title and register the mortgage, plus any tax on the insurance premium.
Sources.whyCredits: Refunds and credits that reduce the bill — some at closing, some only when you file.
Sources.whyPropTax: A published rate applies to an assessment, which is not always the sale price. Where the two differ, the rate you see is derived, and the derivation is named here.
Sources.whyMarket: Benchmark prices, rents and year-over-year change. Publishers differ on the metric — benchmark, median or average — and each entry says which one it is.
Sources.whyFees: Lawyers, inspectors, movers and insurers price per transaction, and no authority publishes a schedule. Every figure here is a default we chose.
Sources.notesNote: The notes are the verification record, kept in English in the words of whoever checked the figure.
Sources.none: No source recorded for this jurisdiction yet.
